screens.title: Understanding and Managing Binary Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Binary logs are the authoritative record of every data-changing event on a MySQL source server. In this lesson you will learn what a binary log records, the differences between STATEMENT, ROW and MIXED formats, why the choice matters for replication consistency, and how to configure and maintain binary logs so replicas can stay synchronized. We will look at my. cnf settings like enabling log_bin, setting binlog_format, controlling retention with expire_logs_days, and rotating files with max_binlog_size. You will also see how to use the mysqlbinlog utility to inspect actual INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE events and how to purge old files safely without breaking replication. Understanding these details prevents divergence, eases audits and keeps disk usage predictable. By the end, you will be able to choose an appropriate format, verify log files, read events for debugging, and decide when and how to purge with confidence. Consider this chapter your practical guide to managing the data-change ledger of MySQL.

screens.title: What the Binary Log Records
screens.narratorSegment: The binary log is a sequential, durable record of every event that modifies data on the source server. It contains transaction boundaries — such as BEGIN and COMMIT — and the events inside those transactions that change rows or execute statements. When a replica connects, it reads and replays these events to apply the same changes. This makes the binlog central to replication, point-in-time recovery, and auditing. A concrete example: when you insert a row into a users table, the binary log contains an event describing that insertion. In ROW format you will see the actual row values written; in STATEMENT format you will see the S Q L used to create the change. A common misconception is to treat the binlog like a human-readable audit trail; while it can be read, its structure is optimized for replication and recovery, not for casual auditing. Always use mysqlbinlog and the correct flags to interpret events. Takeaway: treat the binlog as the single source of truth for data-changing events and plan your replication and backup strategies around its retention and availability. How would losing a range of binlog files affect your replication topology?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What the Binary Log Records
Definition and purpose
A sequential record of data-modifying events and transaction boundaries used for replication and recovery.
What you see in logs
  • Transaction markers such as BEGIN and COMMIT.
  • Events: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements or row images.
  • Metadata: table identifiers, schema names and positions for replication tracking.
Concrete example
In ROW format: an UPDATE records the old row and the new row values so the replica applies identical changes regardless of nondeterministic SQL.
Common misconception
The binlog is not primarily a human audit; it is designed for exact replay. Use mysqlbinlog for interpretation rather than ad hoc reading.
Key Takeaway

Treat the binlog as the canonical, replayable stream of data modifications. Losing files can force re-initialization of replicas.

Visual: event types
Example of a simplified mysqlbinlog snippet showing transaction markers and an UPDATE event in row format.
# at 1234
#200101 12:00:00 server id 1  end_log_pos 1300  Query   thread_id=1  exec_time=0  error_code=0
SET TIMESTAMP=1609459200;
BEGIN
# at 1300
#200101 12:00:01 server id 1  end_log_pos 1500  Write_rows: table_id=123 flags: STMT_END_F
### INSERT INTO `binlog_test`.`users`
### SET
###   @1=1 /* id */
###   @2='Alice' /* name */
###   @3='alice@example.com' /* email */
COMMIT

screens.title: STATEMENT vs ROW vs MIXED
screens.narratorSegment: MySQL supports STATEMENT, ROW and MIXED binlog formats, and the choice drives replication behavior. STATEMENT logs the S Q L statements themselves; it is compact and efficient for simple deterministic statements. However, if a statement is non-deterministic — for example, using functions that return different values like a random selector or current timestamp — STATEMENT can cause replicas to diverge because the statement may produce different results when replayed. ROW logs the before and after images of each affected row, guaranteeing deterministic application on replicas because they apply the same concrete changes. The trade-off is larger log size for multi-row operations. MIXED attempts to balance both: it logs statements by default but switches to row images for statements MySQL marks as unsafe. A concrete example: an UPDATE with ORDER BY RAND() LIMIT 1 is unsafe in STATEMENT because the chosen row could differ; ROW would capture the exact row change. Misconception alert: MIXED does not make all problems invisible — unexpected switches can still complicate analysis. Takeaway: prefer ROW for modern production systems when consistency and predictable replication are priorities.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › STATEMENT vs ROW vs MIXED
Format comparison
Understand behavior, size and determinism trade-offs.
STATEMENT
Logs SQL. Compact. Broken by non-deterministic functions or unordered operations.
ROW
Logs old and new row images. Deterministic and safe for replication. Generates larger logs for many-row changes.
MIXED
Defaults to statement but switches to row for unsafe statements. A compromise with unpredictable switching.
Concrete example
Consider UPDATE ... ORDER BY RAND() LIMIT 1. STATEMENT logs the SQL, reproducing nondeterministic selection on the replica and risking divergence. ROW logs which specific row changed and the new values, so the replica applies identical changes.
Common mistake

Choosing STATEMENT to save space without auditing queries for nondeterminism leads to subtle replication errors later.

Key Takeaway

For modern InnoDB setups with availability requirements, ROW is recommended because it preserves determinism.

screens.title: Configuring binlog parameters in my.cnf
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring binary logging requires careful edits to my. cnf and a controlled restart. Key parameters are log_bin to enable logging and set the base name, binlog_format to choose STATEMENT, ROW or MIXED, expire_logs_days to let MySQL automatically purge older files, and max_binlog_size to rotate files when they grow too large. A concrete example file snippet sets binlog_format to ROW and keeps seven days of logs with a maximum file size. After editing, restart the server and verify with SHOW MASTER STATUS to see the active file name. A common misconception is to set expire_logs_days too low; if replicas lag, required files may be deleted. Another mistake is not aligning retention with backup windows. The practical rule: set expire_logs_days slightly longer than your longest expected replica downtime or backup retention period. Key takeaway: a conservative retention window and appropriate rotation size make it easier to manage storage without risking replication recovery. Configuring binlog parameters in my.cnf means set log_bin and binlog_format in my.cnf, choose expire_logs_days and max_binlog_size to balance retention and disk usage.. In practical terms, enable logging, set format, retention and rotation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Configuring binlog parameters in my.cnf
my.cnf example
Edit these settings and restart MySQL to apply.
[mysqld]
binlog_format = ROW
log_bin = mysql-bin
expire_logs_days = 7
max_binlog_size = 100M
After restart, verify with SHOW MASTER STATUS to record the current file and position for replication tracking.
Notes and cautions
  • expire_logs_days should exceed the longest expected replica downtime.
  • max_binlog_size controls rotation; smaller sizes create more files but simplify transfers.
  • log_bin sets the base name; MySQL appends sequence numbers on rotation.
Common mistake

Setting expire_logs_days too low without checking replica lag can force full re-initialization of replicas when required logs are deleted.

screens.title: Using mysqlbinlog to inspect events
screens.narratorSegment: mysqlbinlog is the primary tool to read binary log files in a human-friendly form. It can display transaction markers, queries, and — when decoding row-based events — the before-and-after images that show exact changes. Useful options include start-position and stop-position to narrow the range of events, the database option to filter events for a specific database, and the base64 decode flag combined with verbose to render row images. A concrete example: run mysqlbinlog with the decode option on the file name reported by SHOW MASTER STATUS to inspect the recent INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE events. When you see BEGIN and COMMIT surrounding events, you can identify transaction boundaries; for row events you will read the table id and the actual column values. A common misconception is to assume mysqlbinlog output always matches application S Q L; in ROW mode you must interpret row images rather than expecting the original S Q L. Takeaway: use mysqlbinlog with the right flags to diagnose replication issues and to extract exact row changes for auditing or recovery. Using mysqlbinlog to inspect events means use mysqlbinlog with --base64-output=decode-rows and -v to view row-based events and transaction boundaries for auditing and debugging.. In practical terms, commands for decoding row events and filtering by position or database. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Using mysqlbinlog to inspect events
Common mysqlbinlog workflows
Use these commands to read and filter events.
# View an entire binary log
mysqlbinlog mysql-bin.000001

# View events from specific positions
mysqlbinlog --start-position=1234 --stop-position=5678 mysql-bin.000001

# Decode row-based events for readability
mysqlbinlog --base64-output=decode-rows -v mysql-bin.000001
Reading results
Look for BEGIN and COMMIT to identify transactions. For row events, verify table identifiers and the before/after column values to reconstruct exactly what changed.
Pro tip

Pipe mysqlbinlog output to less for easier navigation, and decode rows when inspecting ROW-format logs to avoid misinterpreting binary data.

Exercise card

Locate an INSERT and an UPDATE for a test table in the mysqlbinlog output and confirm whether the UPDATE shows before and after values when using ROW format.

screens.title: Identifying the active binary log and positions
screens.narratorSegment: Knowing which binary log file is active and the current write position is essential for replication setup and troubleshooting. On the source, the SHOW MASTER STATUS command reports the current binary log file name and position. Use that file name when running mysqlbinlog and when recording a consistent backup position. For replicas, use SHOW REPLICA STATUS to inspect the Source_Log_File and Source_Log_Pos fields or the Retrieved_Gtid_Set to know what events are required to catch up. A practical example: after making a snapshot backup, note the file and position from SHOW MASTER STATUS so you can configure a replica to start replaying from that point. A common mistake is trusting expire settings without checking replica positions; automatic expiry can remove files that replicas still need. Takeaway: always obtain and record the master file and position when performing backups or before purging binlogs, and cross-check replica status to avoid orphaned replicas that require full re-initialization. Identifying the active binary log and positions means use show master status to capture the current file and position for backups; check show replica status on replicas before purging logs.. In practical terms, show master status and replica position checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Identifying the active binary log and positions
Master and Replica checks
Capture these values before backups and purges.
-- On the source server
SHOW MASTER STATUS;

-- On a replica
SHOW REPLICA STATUS;  -- inspect Source_Log_File and Source_Log_Pos or Retrieved_Gtid_Set
Record the file and position from SHOW MASTER STATUS when taking logical backups so replicas can start from that exact point without missing or replaying events out of order.
Checklist before purge
  • Run SHOW REPLICA STATUS on all replicas and confirm they do not need older files.
  • Confirm backup retention windows align with expire_logs_days.
  • Document the latest master file and position for recovery.
Common mistake

Not checking all replicas before purging. A late or offline replica may still need older binary logs.

screens.title: Purging binary logs safely
screens.narratorSegment: Purging binary logs is necessary to reclaim disk space, but it must be done with careful checks. MySQL provides expire_logs_days to automatically remove older binary logs after a configured number of days. However, automatic expiry will not remove files still required by any connected replica. Manual purging using the PURGE BINARY LOGS statement allows finer control. You can purge up to a specified file name or before a given timestamp. A careful workflow: first run SHOW REPLICA STATUS on every replica to find the oldest file still needed; then either increase expire_logs_days conservatively or issue PURGE BINARY LOGS TO with the most recent safe filename. Concrete example commands include PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'mysql-bin.000005' or PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE with a timestamp. A common mistake is to purge without confirming replica positions, which leaves replicas unable to catch up and forces full re-initialization. Takeaway: always verify replica state first and purge only logs older than the oldest required by any replica. Purging binary logs safely means automatic expiry helps, but manual purge requires confirming replica positions to prevent broken replication.. In practical terms, automatic expiry vs manual purge and safety checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Working with binary logs includes several recurring pitfalls. First, purging logs without checking all replica positions is the most damaging mistake; it causes replicas to lose the ability to catch up and forces a full re-initialization. Second, setting expire_logs_days too aggressively to save disk quickly can have the same effect when replicas are offline longer than expected. Third, assuming STATEMENT format is always fine because it is compact overlooks nondeterministic functions and queries that depend on row ordering; such queries break replication consistency. Fourth, failing to enable log_bin on a prospective replica that might become a source in a failover can limit future recovery or chain replication options. To avoid these issues, always check SHOW REPLICA STATUS on each replica before purging, set expire_ticks conservatively relative to backup windows, prefer ROW for safety in production, and enable log_bin on any server that could act as a source. Takeaway: conservative defaults and verifying replica state prevent costly outages and data divergence. Common mistakes and safety considerations means always verify replica positions before purging and favor conservative retention and row format to prevent replication divergence.. fullNarratorScript:
Binary logs are the authoritative record of every data-changing event on a MySQL source server. In this lesson you will learn what a binary log records, the differences between STATEMENT, ROW and MIXED formats, why the choice matters for replication consistency, and how to configure and maintain binary logs so replicas can stay synchronized. We will look at my. cnf settings like enabling log_bin, setting binlog_format, controlling retention with expire_logs_days, and rotating files with max_binlog_size. You will also see how to use the mysqlbinlog utility to inspect actual INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE events and how to purge old files safely without breaking replication. Understanding these details prevents divergence, eases audits and keeps disk usage predictable. By the end, you will be able to choose an appropriate format, verify log files, read events for debugging, and decide when and how to purge with confidence. Consider this chapter your practical guide to managing the data-change ledger of MySQL.

Over the next slides you will learn a sequence of practical competencies for working with MySQL binary logs. First, you will explain the three binlog formats and how each affects replication behavior and performance. Second, you will configure the key binary-log parameters in my. cnf, such as enabling log_bin, choosing binlog_format, and setting retention and rotation values. Third, you will use the mysqlbinlog utility to inspect file contents, decode row-based events, and locate INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE events for troubleshooting. Fourth, you will implement safe purging strategies: how to check replica positions and how to decide when to use PURGE BINARY LOGS or rely on expire logs. Each objective includes a brief mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you can confirm mastery. These skills matter because the binlog is the fundamental data-change ledger; misconfigurations or premature purges lead to broken replication and costly re-initialization. Practice inspecting a test binlog and verifying replica status to prove you can manage logs safely.

These objectives focus on concrete tasks you will perform to prove competency. You will edit my. cnf to enable binary logging and set binlog_format, then restart the server to verify the active format. You will use SHOW MASTER STATUS to identify the current binary log file and position. Using mysqlbinlog with the base64-decode option and verbose mode, you will find INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE events and interpret before-and-after row images. Finally, you will exercise safe purging: learn to inspect replica positions via SHOW REPLICA STATUS and decide whether automatic expiry is sufficient or a manual PURGE is necessary. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can check your work, for example, confirming that mysqlbinlog output shows row images when ROW format is in use. These skills reduce risk when managing production replication and give you concrete evidence you can operate safely.

The binary log is a sequential, durable record of every event that modifies data on the source server. It contains transaction boundaries — such as BEGIN and COMMIT — and the events inside those transactions that change rows or execute statements. When a replica connects, it reads and replays these events to apply the same changes. This makes the binlog central to replication, point-in-time recovery, and auditing. A concrete example: when you insert a row into a users table, the binary log contains an event describing that insertion. In ROW format you will see the actual row values written; in STATEMENT format you will see the S Q L used to create the change. A common misconception is to treat the binlog like a human-readable audit trail; while it can be read, its structure is optimized for replication and recovery, not for casual auditing. Always use mysqlbinlog and the correct flags to interpret events. Takeaway: treat the binlog as the single source of truth for data-changing events and plan your replication and backup strategies around its retention and availability. How would losing a range of binlog files affect your replication topology?

MySQL supports STATEMENT, ROW and MIXED binlog formats, and the choice drives replication behavior. STATEMENT logs the S Q L statements themselves; it is compact and efficient for simple deterministic statements. However, if a statement is non-deterministic — for example, using functions that return different values like a random selector or current timestamp — STATEMENT can cause replicas to diverge because the statement may produce different results when replayed. ROW logs the before and after images of each affected row, guaranteeing deterministic application on replicas because they apply the same concrete changes. The trade-off is larger log size for multi-row operations. MIXED attempts to balance both: it logs statements by default but switches to row images for statements MySQL marks as unsafe. A concrete example: an UPDATE with ORDER BY RAND() LIMIT 1 is unsafe in STATEMENT because the chosen row could differ; ROW would capture the exact row change. Misconception alert: MIXED does not make all problems invisible — unexpected switches can still complicate analysis. Takeaway: prefer ROW for modern production systems when consistency and predictable replication are priorities.

Configuring binary logging requires careful edits to my. cnf and a controlled restart. Key parameters are log_bin to enable logging and set the base name, binlog_format to choose STATEMENT, ROW or MIXED, expire_logs_days to let MySQL automatically purge older files, and max_binlog_size to rotate files when they grow too large. A concrete example file snippet sets binlog_format to ROW and keeps seven days of logs with a maximum file size. After editing, restart the server and verify with SHOW MASTER STATUS to see the active file name. A common misconception is to set expire_logs_days too low; if replicas lag, required files may be deleted. Another mistake is not aligning retention with backup windows. The practical rule: set expire_logs_days slightly longer than your longest expected replica downtime or backup retention period. Key takeaway: a conservative retention window and appropriate rotation size make it easier to manage storage without risking replication recovery. Configuring binlog parameters in my.cnf means set log_bin and binlog_format in my.cnf, choose expire_logs_days and max_binlog_size to balance retention and disk usage.. In practical terms, enable logging, set format, retention and rotation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

mysqlbinlog is the primary tool to read binary log files in a human-friendly form. It can display transaction markers, queries, and — when decoding row-based events — the before-and-after images that show exact changes. Useful options include start-position and stop-position to narrow the range of events, the database option to filter events for a specific database, and the base64 decode flag combined with verbose to render row images. A concrete example: run mysqlbinlog with the decode option on the file name reported by SHOW MASTER STATUS to inspect the recent INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE events. When you see BEGIN and COMMIT surrounding events, you can identify transaction boundaries; for row events you will read the table id and the actual column values. A common misconception is to assume mysqlbinlog output always matches application S Q L; in ROW mode you must interpret row images rather than expecting the original S Q L. Takeaway: use mysqlbinlog with the right flags to diagnose replication issues and to extract exact row changes for auditing or recovery. Using mysqlbinlog to inspect events means use mysqlbinlog with --base64-output=decode-rows and -v to view row-based events and transaction boundaries for auditing and debugging.. In practical terms, commands for decoding row events and filtering by position or database. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Knowing which binary log file is active and the current write position is essential for replication setup and troubleshooting. On the source, the SHOW MASTER STATUS command reports the current binary log file name and position. Use that file name when running mysqlbinlog and when recording a consistent backup position. For replicas, use SHOW REPLICA STATUS to inspect the Source_Log_File and Source_Log_Pos fields or the Retrieved_Gtid_Set to know what events are required to catch up. A practical example: after making a snapshot backup, note the file and position from SHOW MASTER STATUS so you can configure a replica to start replaying from that point. A common mistake is trusting expire settings without checking replica positions; automatic expiry can remove files that replicas still need. Takeaway: always obtain and record the master file and position when performing backups or before purging binlogs, and cross-check replica status to avoid orphaned replicas that require full re-initialization. Identifying the active binary log and positions means use show master status to capture the current file and position for backups; check show replica status on replicas before purging logs.. In practical terms, show master status and replica position checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Purging binary logs is necessary to reclaim disk space, but it must be done with careful checks. MySQL provides expire_logs_days to automatically remove older binary logs after a configured number of days. However, automatic expiry will not remove files still required by any connected replica. Manual purging using the PURGE BINARY LOGS statement allows finer control. You can purge up to a specified file name or before a given timestamp. A careful workflow: first run SHOW REPLICA STATUS on every replica to find the oldest file still needed; then either increase expire_logs_days conservatively or issue PURGE BINARY LOGS TO with the most recent safe filename. Concrete example commands include PURGE BINARY LOGS TO 'mysql-bin.000005' or PURGE BINARY LOGS BEFORE with a timestamp. A common mistake is to purge without confirming replica positions, which leaves replicas unable to catch up and forces full re-initialization. Takeaway: always verify replica state first and purge only logs older than the oldest required by any replica. Purging binary logs safely means automatic expiry helps, but manual purge requires confirming replica positions to prevent broken replication.. In practical terms, automatic expiry vs manual purge and safety checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Working with binary logs includes several recurring pitfalls. First, purging logs without checking all replica positions is the most damaging mistake; it causes replicas to lose the ability to catch up and forces a full re-initialization. Second, setting expire_logs_days too aggressively to save disk quickly can have the same effect when replicas are offline longer than expected. Third, assuming STATEMENT format is always fine because it is compact overlooks nondeterministic functions and queries that depend on row ordering; such queries break replication consistency. Fourth, failing to enable log_bin on a prospective replica that might become a source in a failover can limit future recovery or chain replication options. To avoid these issues, always check SHOW REPLICA STATUS on each replica before purging, set expire_ticks conservatively relative to backup windows, prefer ROW for safety in production, and enable log_bin on any server that could act as a source. Takeaway: conservative defaults and verifying replica state prevent costly outages and data divergence. Summarizing key ideas helps lock in safe practices. First, the binary log is the authoritative record of data-changing events used by replicas to remain synchronized; losing required files forces replica re-initialization. Second, binlog_format selection matters: STATEMENT logs S Q L, ROW logs concrete row images and is recommended for deterministic replication in modern setups, and MIXED attempts to balance both. Third, configuration and lifecycle parameters — log_bin, expire_logs_days and max_binlog_size — control enabling, retention and rotation. Fourth, mysqlbinlog with decode-rows and verbose is the tool to read row images and transaction markers for auditing and debugging. Finally, always verify replica status before purging. These points together guide safe operation: prefer ROW for consistency, verify state before purge, and use mysqlbinlog to inspect exact changes.
